section.title: He Put a New Song in My Mouth
section.sectionRationale: David moves from testimony of a past rescue, being lifted from the pit and given a new song, to a declaration that obedience, not mere sacrifice, is what God desires, and finally to an urgent plea for present help. The Letter to the Hebrews quotes verses 6-8 directly as the words of Christ Himself entering the world.
section.thesis: David testifies that the LORD lifted him from the pit and put a new song of praise in his mouth, and declares that God desires a heart that delights to do His will rather than mere sacrifice, words the New Testament places directly in the mouth of Jesus as He comes to do the Father's will once for all.
section.frameNote: Four movements: testimony of rescue and a new song, verses 1-3; the blessing of trusting the LORD and the wonders He has done, verses 4-5; the declaration that obedience, not sacrifice, is what God desires, verses 6-10; and the closing plea for present help amid overwhelming trouble, verses 11-17.

units.label: He put a new song in my mouth

verses.text: I waited patiently for the LORD; He inclined to me and heard my cry.
He lifted me up from the pit of despair, out of the miry clay; He set my feet upon a rock, and made my footsteps firm.
He put a new song in my mouth, a hymn of praise to our God. Many will see and fear and put their trust in the LORD.

units.label: Blessed is the man who trusts the Lord

verses.text: Blessed is the man who has made the LORD his trust, who has not turned to the proud, nor to those who lapse into falsehood.
Many, O LORD my God, are the wonders You have done, and the plans You have for us, none can compare to You, if I proclaim and declare them, they are more than I can count.

units.label: I delight to do Your will

verses.text: Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but my ears You have {{karah|opened}}. Burnt offerings and sin offerings You did not require.
Then I said, "Here I am, I have come, it is written about me in the scroll:
I delight to do Your will, O my God; Your law is within my heart."

I proclaim righteousness in the great assembly; behold, I do not seal my lips, 
as You, O LORD, do know.
I have not covered up Your righteousness in my heart; I have declared Your faithfulness and salvation; I have not concealed Your loving devotion and faithfulness from the great assembly.

units.label: Be pleased, O Lord, to deliver me

verses.text: O LORD, do not withhold Your mercy from me; Your loving devotion and faithfulness will always guard me.
For evils without number surround me; my sins have overtaken me, so that I cannot see. They are more than the hairs of my head, and my heart has failed within me.
Be pleased, O LORD, to deliver me; hurry, O LORD, to help me.
May those who seek my life be ashamed and confounded; may those who wish me harm be repelled and humiliated.
May those who say to me, "Aha, aha!" be appalled at their own shame.
May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You; may those who love Your salvation always say, "The LORD be magnified!"
But I am poor and needy; may the Lord think of me. You are my helper and deliverer; O my God, do not delay.

karah.gloss: Literally 'ears You have dug,' picturing God opening or piercing the ear to hear and obey, an image the Greek Septuagint renders as 'a body You have prepared for me,' the very form quoted in Hebrews 10:5 of Christ's incarnation.

basic.context: David testifies to a past rescue, lifted from a miry pit, given a new song, and moves to the heart of true worship: God does not ultimately desire sacrifice and offering but a heart that delights to do His will, 'Here I am, I have come.' The psalm then turns to present, urgent need, surrounded by evils and sins, pleading for God's quick help even while trusting His steadfast love.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm holds together testimony of past deliverance, a theology of true worship as obedient delight rather than ritual performance, and honest present lament, teaching that remembering God's past faithfulness fuels present hope rather than replacing the need for it.
basic.originalLanguages: Verse 6's striking phrase, 'my ears You have opened,' literally 'dug,' pictures God piercing the ear to hear and obey rather than merely perform ritual. The Greek Old Testament renders this 'a body You have prepared for me,' the very wording Hebrews 10:5 places on Christ's lips as He enters the world.
basic.typology: David's declaration, 'Here I am, I have come... I delight to do Your will,' functions typologically as the pattern, and in Hebrews 10:5-7 explicitly as the very words, of Christ's obedient incarnation, coming to do what sacrifices and offerings alone could never accomplish.
basic.christ: Hebrews 10:5-7 quotes this psalm's verses 6-8 directly as the words Christ speaks entering the world: 'Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but a body You have prepared for Me... Then I said, Here I am, I have come, it is written of Me in the scroll, I have come to do Your will, O God.' What David could only foreshadow in his own obedient life, Christ fulfills completely, His body offered once for all replacing every sacrifice that could never truly take away sin.
basic.god: God is shown as one who values a heart that delights in obedience over the mere performance of ritual sacrifice, and as the faithful helper whose steadfast love and faithfulness will always guard those who trust Him, even amid overwhelming present trouble.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 10:5-10 quotes this psalm directly, showing Christ's incarnation and obedience fulfilling and superseding the entire sacrificial system. 1 Samuel 15:22 similarly declares that obedience is better than sacrifice. Revelation 5:9 pictures the new song of redemption sung to the Lamb who was slain.
basic.oneStory: David's testimony of rescue, new song, and obedient delight in God's will anticipates Christ, who takes this psalm's very words on His lips in Hebrews 10, coming in a body prepared for Him to do the Father's will fully, offering Himself once for all so that God's people might sing a truly new song of salvation.

context.literary:
Psalm 40 is built in two halves that seem at first to belong to different moods. Verses 1 to 10 are thanksgiving: a rescue told in the past tense, a new song, a beatitude, a confession that God wants obedience more than offerings, and a report of public praise. Verses 11 to 17 are petition: evils without number, sins that have overtaken him, enemies who mock, and a plea for God not to delay. The change happens at verse 11 with a single word, 'You,' set in emphatic place, and the psalmist's prayer runs on the strength of what he has just said.

The two halves are joined by a pair of verbs about what is withheld. In verse 9 the psalmist says he does not 'seal' his lips, in the Hebrew a verb of restraint, and in verse 11 he asks God not to 'withhold' His mercy, with the same verb. The man who has not kept back his praise asks that God not keep back His compassion. The linking is quiet, and it turns the two halves into a single argument: what I have done in praise I ask You to do in mercy.

The first half moves in a clear order. It tells the story of rescue in three steps, verses 1 to 3, sets a beatitude on trust in verse 4, marvels at God's wonders in verse 5, and then makes the pivotal turn to the theology of sacrifice in verses 6 to 8. Verses 9 and 10 answer by the psalmist's vow of public witness, and in those two verses four terms, righteousness, faithfulness, salvation and loving devotion, are heaped up. The last five verses, 13 to 17, appear again almost word for word as Psalm 70, with small changes in the divine name, and this doubling has led many readers to ask whether the psalm is a unity or two prayers joined.
context.historical:
The psalm gives us a king in the setting of the temple courts. 'The great assembly,' verses 9 and 10, means the gathered congregation at the sanctuary, where Israelites brought their thank offerings and told of what God had done. The story of the pit and the miry clay, verse 2, borrows the language of a dungeon or a cistern, a place from which no man climbs out alone, and the psalmist's rescue from it would have been told before witnesses. Psalm 30:2-3 tells of a man pulled up from Sheol in similar terms.

The heart of the psalm is the statement that God did not desire 'sacrifice and offering,' verse 6, naming four categories of the Levitical system: the peace or fellowship offering, the grain offering, the burnt offering and the sin offering. A first hearer in David's Israel lived with these daily. To hear that God did not 'desire' or 'require' them would not have sounded like an abolition of the cult. It would have sounded like the prophets' word that ritual without obedience is empty, 1 Samuel 15:22 and Hosea 6:6, and like the psalmist's own word in Psalm 51:16-17 that God's real sacrifice is a broken spirit.

'The scroll' of verse 7 evokes the book of the Law. The king of Israel was to write for himself a copy of the Law and read it all his days, Deuteronomy 17:18-20, and this may be what stands behind the phrase 'it is written about me.' The psalmist is a king in the presence of the scroll that governs kings. Verse 8, 'Your law is within my heart,' is the ideal of the Law's purpose, that it should be interior, Psalm 37:31, and it anticipates the new covenant promise of Jeremiah 31:33.

The conflict in the second half is ordinary politics: enemies who 'seek my life,' who say 'Aha, aha!' in the mocking style of Psalm 35:21, and a king under pressure with his own sins pressing on him, verse 12.
context.canonical:
Psalm 40 is one of the most quoted psalms in the New Testament, though only in one place by direct citation. Hebrews 10:5-10 takes verses 6 to 8 and places them in the mouth of Christ as He 'came into the world,' and builds a whole argument on them. The BSB footnote at verse 6 records the difference that makes the argument possible: the Hebrew says 'ears You have opened' and the Greek translation Hebrews follows says 'a body You prepared for me.' The link is made at the note on verse 8, 'Cited in Hebrews 10:5-7.'

Within the Old Testament, the psalm belongs to a strand that sets obedience above offering: Samuel's word to Saul, 1 Samuel 15:22, Hosea's 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice,' Hosea 6:6, Psalm 51:16-17, and Micah's list of the things the LORD requires, Micah 6:6-8. The 'new song' of verse 3 also recurs across the Psalter, Psalms 33:3, 96:1 and 98:1, and in Revelation 5:9, where the redeemed sing a new song to the Lamb who was slain.

The psalm has close relations with the psalms around it. It picks up the waiting of Psalm 39:7, 'for what do I wait,' with 'I waited patiently,' using the verb of waiting that 39:7 asks about, now given its answer. Verses 13 to 17 return in Psalm 70 almost word for word, and the Psalter's compilers plainly wanted both prayers to be sung. The passage on the poor and needy, verse 17, also recurs in Psalms 86:1 and 109:22. And the psalm feeds into Psalm 41, which follows, in the theme of the one who thinks of the weak, 41:1, and of God's 'thinking' of the psalmist, 40:17.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist meant his hearers to learn that gratitude has to be spoken, and that the deepest gratitude looks like obedience. He tells a story of rescue not for his own credit but so that 'many will see and fear and put their trust in the LORD,' verse 3. His testimony is an act of service to the assembly, a public gift that stands in place of a private feeling.

He also meant to make a claim about worship. The cult had its place; the psalm does not throw it out. But a man who brings an offering and has not given his ears, his heart and his will has brought nothing that God wanted. The 'ears' God has dug for him are the mark of a servant, and 'Your law is within my heart' is the sign of one who does what he is told out of love.

A third aim is to hold together thanks and need. The second half of the psalm, with its cry of sins that outnumber his hairs and his failing heart, was not meant to undercut the first. It was meant to show that a man who has been rescued still needs rescue, and that the past is the ground on which to pray. The psalmist argues from what God has done to what he asks God to do, and his confidence rests on God's character, 'Your loving devotion and faithfulness will always guard me,' verse 11.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records the psalmist's testimony and his prayers. It does not command that anyone must sing publicly of a specific rescue, but it clearly commends the practice, and the New Testament builds on it, 1 Peter 2:9. It does not abolish sacrifice on its own account, since Israel's sacrifices were commanded by God. What it prescribes is the priority: obedience from the heart is what God is after, and sacrifice without it is empty.

Hebrews takes the psalm a step further. The letter says that the sacrificial system, which was a shadow of good things to come, 'can never ... take away sins,' Hebrews 10:1-4, and that Christ's offering, 'once for all,' has set it aside, Hebrews 10:10. This is a description of what has happened in the history of salvation, not a permission for believers to dismiss the Old Testament. The Old Testament sacrifices had their proper work as shadows and teachers, and readers who see them fulfilled in Christ read them more truly, not less.

The confession of verse 12 is also descriptive. The psalmist does not offer a doctrine of sin, and he certainly does not urge believers to keep counting their sins. He is honest about a condition. The right application is to bring that honesty to God, as he does, and to take heart in the answer in the same psalm, that the LORD 'will always guard' the one who runs to Him.

debates.question: Who is speaking in verses 6 to 8, and how does Hebrews 10 use them?

views.label: David speaking of himself, with Hebrews reading the pattern typologically
views.case: The psalm is a first person prayer of a king with 'my sins' in verse 12. Hebrews reads David's words as the pattern that Jesus fulfills, in the way the apostles often read the Psalms of David as anticipating the Son of David. The 'body' of the Greek version fits Hebrews' point that God prepared a bodily obedience.

views.label: Christ speaking prophetically through David
views.case: Hebrews introduces the citation with 'when Christ came into the world, He said,' Hebrews 10:5, treating the words as spoken by the Son to the Father. On this view David is a prophet, as Peter says of him in Acts 2:30-31, and the psalm's deepest voice is the Messiah. The difficulty is verse 12, 'my sins have overtaken me,' which is harder to put on His lips, though many suggest that He speaks of sins He took as His own by imputation, and Augustine's habit was to hear Christ speaking with His body, the church.

views.label: The righteous king, representing the faithful in Israel
views.case: Some see the speaker as the Davidic king who stands for the godly of Israel, so that the psalm is at once personal and representative. The New Testament would then apply it to the one Davidic King who fully realises the pattern.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that Hebrews found in the psalm a real word about obedience and body. The safest reading keeps David as the first speaker and Christ as the one in whom the pattern is complete, and hears verse 12 as the confession of David and the burden Christ took.

debates.question: Is the psalm one prayer or two joined together?

views.label: Two originally separate pieces
views.case: The change of mood at verse 11 is abrupt, from thanksgiving to lament, and verses 13 to 17 stand as a separate psalm in Psalm 70 with changes such as 'God' for 'LORD' in some places. On this view an editor joined a thanksgiving to a short lament or borrowed a lament to end a thanksgiving.

views.label: One prayer, thanks becoming the ground for petition
views.case: The Hebrew links between the halves, the verb for 'seal' and 'withhold' in verses 9 and 11, and the shared words for loving devotion and faithfulness in verses 10 and 11, suggest a planned unity. Psalm 30 and Psalm 27 also move from thanksgiving to petition, and it is ordinary in the Psalter for past deliverance to be used as an argument for present help.

debates.bearing: Whatever the history of its composition, the psalm as it stands teaches that testimony and petition belong in the same prayer. Remembering rescue does not end the need to ask again, it gives the asking its courage.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb of verse 6 is karah, which the BSB translates 'opened' and which is elsewhere used of digging: a pit is dug with it, Psalm 7:15. The psalmist says God has dug or hollowed out his ears. The common view is that this means God has made him able to hear and obey, in contrast to the sacrifices that God did not want, and that it is related to Isaiah 50:5, 'The Lord GOD has opened My ears,' although Isaiah uses a different verb. It is not the verb of the slave's ear pierced with an awl in Exodus 21:5-6, and that difference matters, because a reader who links this phrase to the slave who loves his master must keep in mind that the words are not the same.

The Hebrew says 'ears,' and Hebrews quotes the Greek version, which says 'a body You prepared for me.' The verb 'prepared' in Hebrews 10:5 is a word for fitting or equipping. Whatever the origin of the Greek reading, whether a way of saying that the whole obedient person is meant or a different text before the translators, the New Testament takes it as an accurate expression of what God did in the incarnation.

The verb for 'delight' has a small story of its own. In verse 6 God did not 'desire' sacrifice, in the Hebrew a verb of delight, chafets, and in verse 8 the psalmist says 'I delight,' with the same root, to do God's will. In verse 14 the enemies 'wish me harm,' again from the same root, and in Psalm 41:11 the psalmist says 'You delight in me.' The verb runs through the psalm as a measure of what each party wants: God does not want offerings, the psalmist wants God's will, the enemies want his hurt.

Verse 9 says 'I proclaim righteousness,' using basar, the verb of bringing good news, the root that gives the Christian word gospel its background. Verse 10 heaps four terms, righteousness, faithfulness, salvation, and 'loving devotion and faithfulness,' the last a pair, chesed and emet, that returns in verse 11 as the ground of protection. Verse 17 says 'may the Lord think of me,' using chashav, the same verb whose noun form gives the 'plans' of verse 5. The many plans God has 'for us' become a thought of God 'for me.'

Verse 1 opens with an intensive form, literally 'waiting I waited,' rendered 'patiently.' Verse 3's 'see and fear' pairs two verbs that sound alike in Hebrew, so that the onlookers 'see' and 'fear' and 'trust' in a single rush of related sounds.

typology.type: The delight in God's will, verses 7 and 8
typology.fulfillment: The psalmist says 'Here I am, I have come ... I delight to do Your will, O my God; Your law is within my heart.' Hebrews puts these words on the lips of Christ at His coming, Hebrews 10:5-7, and adds, 'He takes away the first to establish the second,' verse 9. Jesus said, 'My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work,' John 4:34. The correspondence is complete obedience from the heart. The type falls short because David's obedience was partial and he had sins, verse 12, while Christ's was perfect, and His obedience did what animal sacrifice could never do, Hebrews 10:4.

typology.type: The rescue from the pit, verses 1 and 2
typology.fulfillment: A man is lifted from the pit and the miry clay and set on a rock. The Old Testament often uses such language for deliverance from death, Psalm 30:2-3, and the pattern is fulfilled in the resurrection of Christ, who was brought up from the grave and set at the right hand of God, Hebrews 10:12. Believers share it, since 'God raised us up with Christ and seated us with Him in the heavenly realms,' Ephesians 2:6. The escalation is that David was rescued back into a life that would end, while Christ was raised to a life that cannot. The type falls short because David's rock was firm ground in this world, and Christ's is the seat of the world to come.

God puts a new song in the psalmist's mouth, 'a hymn of praise to our God.' In Revelation 5:9 the redeemed sing a new song to the Lamb: 'Worthy are You to take the scroll and open its seals, because You were slain.' The correspondence is that rescue produces song. The escalation is that the song moves from one man's deliverance to a chorus of people 'from every tribe and tongue and people and nation.' The type falls short because David's song was for his own rescue and for those who would hear it in the temple, while the last song is for the rescue of a whole redeemed humanity.

typology.type: The burnt offerings that could not satisfy, verse 6
typology.fulfillment: Sacrifice and offering, burnt offerings and sin offerings, are set aside in the psalm as not what God wants for their own sake. Hebrews says they were a shadow, an annual reminder of sins, and that 'it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins,' Hebrews 10:1-4. The escalation is the single offering of Christ's body, 'once for all,' verse 10. The correspondence lies in the way the psalm already saw through the system to something more; the type falls short because the sacrifices were commanded and real in their time, and were not empty.

study.christ:
Hebrews 10:5-10 is the plainest link between this psalm and Christ, and it deserves to be read slowly. The writer says that when Christ came into the world He said, 'Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but a body You prepared for Me.' The psalm's verses 6 to 8 are given to the Son as words spoken at His coming, and the writer's comment is that the two sentences stand in a sequence: 'He takes away the first to establish the second,' Hebrews 10:9. The first is the system of sacrifices, the second is the will of God to be done, and 'by that will, we have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all,' verse 10. The whole point of the incarnation, on this reading, is that the Son took a body in order to offer obedience in it.

The idea of a body prepared is not tacked on. Paul says the Son was 'born of a woman, born under the law,' Galatians 4:4, and that He 'humbled Himself and became obedient to death, even death on a cross,' Philippians 2:8. The delight of Psalm 40:8, 'I delight to do Your will,' is what stands behind Jesus' word, 'My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me,' John 4:34, and behind His prayer in Gethsemane, 'not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39. The 'ears' God opened for the psalmist find their perfect use in the Servant of Isaiah 50:5, who says the Lord GOD 'has opened My ears, and I have not been rebellious.'

The psalm also leads to Christ by its structure of rescue. The pit and clay and rock of verses 2 and 3 are read by the New Testament as the pattern of resurrection, and the new song is the song of the redeemed to the Lamb in Revelation 5:9. The psalmist's promise to declare God's righteousness in the great assembly is fulfilled in the Gospel proclaimed to all nations.

The cries of the second half, 'evils without number surround me; my sins have overtaken me,' raise the question of how they fit. Jesus had no sin, yet He bore ours, 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. Some have heard verse 12 as the voice of the Head speaking for His body, and this is a legitimate way to hold the psalm together. The safer course is to say that the psalm is first David's and finds its climax in Christ, who took David's guilt and ours.

A caution: not every line of the psalm should be pushed into Christ's mouth. The psalm's own warrant lies in the link to verses 6 to 8 that the New Testament itself makes. The rest of the psalm is read best as the prayer of the one who needs the Christ that the middle of the psalm anticipates.
study.god:
The God of Psalm 40 is the God who inclines. 'He inclined to me and heard my cry,' verse 1, pictures a person bending down to listen. The Creator does not send His answer from a height; He stoops. The whole rescue in verses 2 and 3, the lifting, the setting on a rock, the steadying of steps, is the work of a hand that reaches down. Before any praise from the psalmist, God is the one who comes near.

He is the God whose works cannot be numbered. Verse 5 says 'many, O LORD my God, are the wonders You have done, and the plans You have for us, none can compare to You ... they are more than I can count.' The psalmist reaches for the same idea as Psalm 139:17-18, that God's thoughts outnumber the grains of sand. God's plans are aimed at His people, 'for us,' and are personal, and in verse 17 they narrow to a single person, 'may the Lord think of me.' His providence is wide enough for the world and close enough for a poor man.

He is a God who wants the heart. The psalm's statement about sacrifice is not a rejection of what He commanded but a disclosure of what He wanted in commanding it. He desired obedient people, 'Your law is within my heart,' verse 8. This fits the God who says through the prophets, 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice,' Hosea 6:6, and the God who tells Samuel that 'obedience is better than sacrifice,' 1 Samuel 15:22. He looks at what the offering means.

He is faithful and loving. Verses 10 and 11 pile up the terms, 'righteousness,' 'faithfulness,' 'salvation,' 'loving devotion,' and use the pair chesed and emet twice. The psalmist bases his hope not on his past obedience but on these attributes, and the attributes are what he has told the assembly. God's character is the stable thing, in a psalm where everything about the psalmist is unstable, his sins outnumbering his hairs and his heart failing.

He is also the God who does not delay. The end of the psalm asks Him to 'hurry' and 'not to delay,' and the urgency is part of the theology. It says that God's help matters in time, on this day, in this need, and that a believer may press Him. It also says the psalmist believes he has a right to pray so: 'You are my helper and deliverer,' verse 17.

For worship, the psalm teaches us to tell what God has done, aloud and among people, and to pray from that memory. It teaches that worship without obedience is a shell. And it teaches that a believer can sing a new song and cry for help in the same breath.

crossReferences.note: The one direct quotation of the psalm in the New Testament. The writer puts verses 6 to 8 in the mouth of Christ as He comes into the world, and argues that He 'takes away the first to establish the second.' The passage turns the psalm's word about sacrifice and obedience into the basis for one final offering.

Samuel tells Saul that 'obedience is better than sacrifice, and attentiveness is better than the fat of rams.' The same priority stands behind Psalm 40:6. The psalm and the story together show that Israel's own history had already set the heart above the ritual before David wrote.

'I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.' The verb of desire is the same in the Hebrew as in Psalm 40:6. The prophet applies the principle to a people whose worship had become empty, and it stands as a witness that the psalm's word is not a new doctrine.

David says God does not delight in sacrifice, or he would bring it, and that His sacrifices are 'a broken spirit.' The wording matches Psalm 40:6 in spirit and in vocabulary. Both psalms come from the same king, and both find God's desire in a heart, not in a gift.

The Servant says, 'The Lord GOD has opened My ears, and I have not been rebellious.' The verb differs from Psalm 40:6, but the picture is the same: a servant whose ears are open to God's word and who obeys. Many readers hear the two passages as complementary portraits of the one obedient Servant.

God promises to 'put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts.' Psalm 40:8, 'Your law is within my heart,' is the experience of one man that the new covenant promises to the whole people. The psalmist anticipates what the Spirit does in every believer.

Jesus says, 'My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work.' It is the psalm's delight in doing God's will spoken in the first person by Christ. The link is one of theme and spirit, and it shows what it looked like when Christ lived Psalm 40:8.

The second half of Psalm 40, verses 13 to 17, appears here almost word for word, with a few changes such as 'Let God be magnified' where Psalm 40 has 'The LORD be magnified.' The doubling shows that the prayer for quick help was treasured and used on its own in worship.

'How vast is their sum! If I were to count them, they would outnumber the grains of sand.' The thoughts of God are beyond counting, as the wonders and plans of Psalm 40:5 are. Both psalmists are overwhelmed by a God whose care for His people exceeds their ability to list it.

'You pulled me up from Sheol; You spared me from descending into the Pit.' It is another testimony of rescue from the pit, told with the language of Psalm 40:2. Together they show how the Psalter spoke of God's saving acts, as being lifted up from the place of death.

The redeemed sing 'a new song' to the Lamb who was slain. Psalm 40:3 tells of a new song put in a mouth by God. The final song is the same gift given at the last: a song God puts in the mouths of those He has redeemed, now sung by a multitude.

'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf.' It helps explain how a psalm with the confession 'my sins have overtaken me' can be read in relation to Christ. The one without sin took up the guilt of others as His own, and so David's cry has a place in His story.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 40 answers a question that runs from Leviticus to the prophets: what does God really want? The Torah gave Israel a system of sacrifice, and the whole story of the Old Testament shows people offering and still failing to obey. The prophets pressed the point, and the psalm gives it its sharpest single line, 'Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but my ears You have opened.' God wanted a people who would hear Him. Since Genesis 3, when the first pair heard a rival voice and stopped listening, the human ear has been the place of the fall, and the psalm sets a hearing ear at the centre of the way back.

The psalm also gathers a promise. God will 'put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts,' Jeremiah 31:33, and the psalmist's line 'Your law is within my heart' is a glimpse of that promised day. His desire, 'I delight to do Your will,' is a sign that obedience from the heart is possible, and yet the second half of the psalm shows he cannot make it complete on his own. The pit and the sins that overtake are the fall's leftovers. That is why the psalm is open at its end, a cry that God not delay.

The story finds its answer in Christ. The Son comes into the world and says, 'Here I am, I have come to do Your will,' Hebrews 10:7. The obedience Adam lacked and Israel could not sustain is offered in a body, and the offering does what sacrifices never could: 'by that will, we have been sanctified,' Hebrews 10:10. The new covenant then writes the law on hearts by the Spirit, and the delight of the psalm becomes the shared experience of the church, Romans 8:4.

The end of the story takes up the song. The new song of verse 3 becomes the song of Revelation 5:9, sung by people from every nation, and the psalm's line 'May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You' comes true when God's people stand before the throne. The pit is left behind, the rock is a city, and those who once had to say 'do not delay' are told 'Yes, I am coming soon,' Revelation 22:20.

sermon.title: What to Do When Your Spirits Sink
sermon.why: Piper preaches directly on Psalm 40:1-3, showing how David's testimony of being lifted from the pit and given a new song models how believers today can wait patiently on the Lord when their own spirits sink, grounding present hope in God's proven, patient faithfulness.

quiz.q: What did the LORD do for David according to verses 1-3?

options.text: He heard David's cry, lifted him from the pit of despair, set his feet on a rock, and put a new song of praise in his mouth.
options.note: This vivid testimony of rescue and renewed praise opens the psalm and grounds everything that follows.

options.text: He ignored David's cry entirely.
options.note: The text explicitly says the LORD inclined to David and heard his cry.

options.text: He punished David further for his sin.
options.note: The passage describes rescue and a new song, not further punishment; sin is addressed later, in verse 12.

options.text: He promised David wealth but withheld rescue.
options.note: The text describes actual deliverance, being lifted from the pit, not merely a promise of future wealth.

quiz.q: What does verse 6 say God desires more than sacrifice and offering?

options.text: Ears opened to hear and obey, a heart that delights to do His will.
options.note: This declaration of obedient delight over ritual sacrifice is the psalm's theological center, quoted directly in Hebrews 10.

options.text: More frequent and elaborate sacrifices.
options.note: The verse explicitly says sacrifice and offering were not what God desired most.

options.text: Silence and withdrawal from worship.
options.note: The following verses describe proclaiming God's righteousness in the great assembly, not withdrawal from worship.

options.text: Wealth given as an offering instead of animals.
options.note: The text contrasts obedient hearts with ritual sacrifice generally, not one form of offering for another.

quiz.q: How does the Letter to the Hebrews use Psalm 40:6-8?

options.text: It quotes these verses directly as the words Christ speaks upon entering the world, His body prepared to do God's will.
options.note: Hebrews 10:5-7 places this psalm's words directly on Christ's lips, showing His incarnation and obedience fulfill it.

options.text: It never references this psalm anywhere.
options.note: Hebrews 10:5-7 quotes Psalm 40:6-8 explicitly and at length.

options.text: It uses the verses to argue that animal sacrifice should continue unchanged.
options.note: Hebrews 10 uses the psalm to argue the opposite, that Christ's one sacrifice ends the need for repeated animal sacrifices.

options.text: It applies the verses only to David personally, with no connection to Christ.
options.note: Hebrews 10:5 explicitly attributes the words to Christ Himself entering the world, not merely to David.

quiz.q: What does David confess about his own condition in verse 12?

options.text: Evils without number surround him and his own sins have overtaken him so that he cannot see, his heart has failed within him.
options.note: This honest confession of present distress and sin follows immediately after his testimony of past obedience and rescue.

options.text: He claims to be entirely free from sin or trouble.
options.note: The text explicitly confesses being overtaken by sins and surrounded by evils, not freedom from trouble.

options.text: He blames only his enemies, admitting no personal sin.
options.note: Verse 12 explicitly says 'my sins have overtaken me,' a personal confession, not only blame directed at enemies.

options.text: He describes only minor, easily managed difficulties.
options.note: The language, 'more than the hairs of my head,' 'my heart has failed,' describes overwhelming, not minor, distress.

quiz.q: How does David describe himself in his closing plea, verse 17?

options.text: As poor and needy, yet confident that the Lord thinks of him and is his helper and deliverer.
options.note: This combination of humble need and confident trust closes the psalm, echoing its opening testimony of rescue.

options.text: As wealthy and self-sufficient, needing no help from God.
options.note: The text explicitly describes David as poor and needy, dependent on God's help.

options.text: As entirely without hope of any deliverance.
options.note: Despite his need, David explicitly expresses confidence that God is his helper and deliverer.

options.text: As angry at God for delaying help.
options.note: While David does ask God not to delay, the tone is urgent trust and petition, not anger at God.

questions: David testifies that God lifted him from a miry pit and gave him a new song. What 'pit' has God rescued you from, and is there a 'new song' of praise you have not yet fully sung about it?
Verse 6 says God desires obedient delight over ritual sacrifice. Where in your life might you be substituting religious performance or activity for a heart that truly delights to do God's will?

Hebrews 10 places David's words, 'Here I am, I have come to do Your will,' directly on the lips of Christ entering the world. How does knowing Jesus spoke these exact words over His own incarnation change how you read David's declaration?

David moves from testimony of past rescue directly into an honest confession of present sin and overwhelming trouble. How can remembering God's past faithfulness help you bring present struggles honestly to Him, rather than hiding them?
The psalm closes, 'I am poor and needy, may the Lord think of me.' Where do you need to trade self-sufficiency for this same honest, humble dependence on God as your helper and deliverer?

translationNotes.note: My ears You have opened translates a Hebrew phrase literally meaning 'ears You have dug,' picturing an ear opened to hear and obey; the Greek Septuagint renders this 'a body You have prepared for me,' the wording Hebrews 10:5 applies to Christ.

It is written about me in the scroll likely refers to the Torah's instructions for the king, or more broadly to Scripture's witness to God's will, which David, and ultimately Christ, comes to fulfill.
These closing verses closely parallel Psalm 70 nearly word for word, suggesting this section may have circulated and been used liturgically as its own psalm of urgent petition.
